Conditional Probability

Probability
Game: This is not a game to win: two coloured rectangles mark two groups of equally likely dots, and the numbers show how likely each group is.
How to play: Drag a corner dot to move or change a rectangle, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Change the grid sizes in the boxes, then press Reset to start over.
P(A) = P(B) = P(A and B) = P(A given B) = P(B given A) =
Look for the math

Two rectangles move over a grid of equally likely dots. Change their size and the readouts change too. The applet's page claims two formulas for conditional probabilities and a test for independence: do they always agree?

Counting the dots

There are Nx × Ny dots, each equally likely. A rectangle covers a whole number of grid cells, so P(A) = cells in A / (Nx × Ny), and the same goes for B. Where the rectangles overlap, that part is counted once: P(A and B) is the number of cells in the overlap divided by all the dots. Corners snap to grid lines, so every displayed number is a fraction of one grid. This is the idea behind probability in a finite sample space.

What “given B” means

If we are told that B happened, only the dots inside B remain possible. Of those, the ones that also lie in A give P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Swapping the letters gives P(B given A) = P(A and B) / P(A). These are the two formulas printed on the applet's page, and the logic test checks all five readouts against a second transcription of the applet's bytecode for every Nx and Ny from 10 to 30. If B has no cells at all, the applet divides zero by zero and displays NaN: the formula needs P(B) > 0. This is the definition of conditional probability.

Independence

The page says A and B are independent when P(A given B) = P(A), which it calls “the same as” P(B given A) = P(B), and adds P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). All three are equivalent when both rectangles have cells: with N = Nx × Ny, each condition is the integer equality overlap × N = cells in A × cells in B. The test confirms this for thousands of rectangles. One caveat: with an empty rectangle a conditional is NaN, so the first two statements cannot be equal while the product statement still holds — the page's “which is the same” silently assumes positive probabilities. Independence in this sense is called statistical independence.

Changing the whole grid

The applet's page gives an independent pair on 25 × 20 dots: A covers 20 cells, B covers 25, and their overlap is 1 cell, so 1/500 = (20/500) × (25/500). Change only the columns to 24 × 20: the same rectangles still give the same two conditional probabilities, but now 1/480 is not (20/480) × (25/480), so the events become dependent. Keeping the conditionals is not enough; the total number of dots matters. The article at the catalogue address (Scott E. Brodie's) makes the related claim that the pieces A ∩ Bᵢ add back up to A, and that P(A) = Σ P(A given Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ) for mutually exclusive, exhaustive Bᵢ — the test checks that identity for every grid here. That article has formulas but no applet; the interactive applet is on the Conditional Probability and Independent Events page, which is the page credited in the byline.

Drag A until it barely touches B, then slide one more cell: watch the overlap readout jump from zero and the two conditional probabilities change together.
